key_insight: Introduce a weight-space metric, tensor similarity, that determines when two tensor-based network modules implement the same computation while being invariant to common weight-space symmetries. This lets researchers verify mechanistic equivalence without relying on behaviour-only tests or fragile basis-dependent comparisons.
problem_solved: Bridges the gap between behavioural similarity (which can miss out-of-distribution equivalence) and raw parameter comparisons (which break under basis/symmetry changes) by providing a symmetry-aware, weight-based test for module-level sameness.
method: Represent model components as tensors and derive a similarity score that is invariant to weight-space symmetries (e.g., permutations, scalings, orthogonal/basis changes) that preserve computation.
Compare modules via symmetry-aware alignment or invariant tensor descriptors rather than elementwise parameter distances, producing a single interpretable similarity metric.
Validate the metric on canonical tensor-based modules and use it to detect mechanistic equivalence that behavioural tests miss (including out-of-distribution cases).
impact: Provides a robust tool for mechanistic interpretability and model analysis: researchers can confidently assert when two subnetworks are functionally the same across models or training runs, improving modular understanding, transfer, and verification.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic of two subnetworks with an arrow showing 'tensor similarity' mapping that ignores permutations/scalings (illustrates invariance).
Heatmap or bar chart of similarity scores across many module pairs, highlighting high/low matches and clusters.
Flowchart showing pipeline: extract tensors → compute symmetry-invariant descriptors/alignment → output similarity score and thresholded equivalence.
Icon set illustrating supported symmetries (permutation, scaling, orthogonal/basis change) with ticks to show invariance.
paper_title: When Are Two Networks the Same? Tensor Similarity for Mechanistic Interpretability
paper_authors: ML Nissen Gonzalez, Melwina Albuquerque, Laurence Wroe, Jacob Meyer Cohen, Logan Riggs Smith
